desc:
Given an array nums of non-negative integers, consider the sum of every subset of its elements (a subset is chosen by index, and the empty subset has sum 0). Different subsets can have the same sum.

Return how many different values occur as the sum of some subset.

[1, 2, 5] -> 8    (sums 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8)
[2, 2, 2] -> 4    (sums 0, 2, 4, 6)
[0, 0]    -> 1    (only the sum 0)
hints: Counting subsets is useless here because many subsets share a sum; you need to count sums.
Maintain the set of sums that are reachable by the elements processed so far. Start with {0}.

When element x comes, the new set is the old set together with {s + x} for every old s. The total never exceeds 20,000, so a boolean array (or a bitset) is enough. The answer is how many entries are true.
editorial: The set of reachable sums only depends on the set from the previous step: after adding element x the reachable sums are the old sums (skip the element) plus the old sums shifted by x (take it). Because every sum lies between 0 and sum(nums) ≤ 20,000, a boolean array indexed by sum represents the set, and one update costs O(sum). In total the cost is O(n · sum).

Zeros change nothing (shifting by 0 gives the same set), and duplicates are handled automatically because we track sums, never subsets. With a big-integer bitset the update is the single statement bits |= bits << x, and the answer is the number of 1-bits.
